contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Transfer when the output objective changes whether a retained entry can be finalized or proved permanently irrelevant before the scan ends.

authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring assistant; human review required

items.prompt: A design review covers Nested delimiters with mixed types. Explain why an unmatched opener remains on an ordinary stack. Which statement gives the decisive justification?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: It is unresolved until the structurally corresponding closer arrives.
It remains because its value is not yet dominated.
Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.
No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.

feedback.reason: It is unresolved until the structurally corresponding closer arrives. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: An opening delimiter creates a structural obligation. A later opener nests inside it but does not make it irrelevant; the older opener must remain until all inner obligations close and its own matching closer reaches the top. For `([ ])`, `(` stays below `[` while `]` resolves only `[`, then `)` resolves `(`. Removal is justified by successful structural matching, not by value dominance. Deleting an older opener when a newer one is pushed would accept crossing or missing pairs, while refusing every early deletion would prevent legitimate closers from consuming completed obligations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Delimiter types define matching obligations, but no numeric-quality relation makes one unmatched opener dominate another.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: A newer nested opener postpones the older obligation; age does not cancel the enclosing scope.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: A matching closer legitimately finalizes and removes the top opener before the scan ends, so permanent retention would be incorrect.

items.prompt: Consider Iterative DFS or explicit recursion simulation. A teammate argues: “A newer frame permanently makes older work irrelevant.” Which response correctly resolves the design decision?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: A newer frame permanently makes older work irrelevant.
Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.
No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.
It represents deferred work to resume after more recent work completes.

feedback.reason: It represents deferred work to resume after more recent work completes. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: An explicit DFS entry represents a node or call frame whose remaining branch work has been deferred. Pushing a child suspends the parent; after the child's frame completes and is popped, the parent or an older sibling is resumed. The newer frame therefore changes execution order but not relevance. Deleting the parent on child push would lose its remaining neighbors or return context. A frame may be removed when all of its scheduled work is complete, which is semantic finalization rather than value dominance. Monotonic pruning would require a different objective proving a newer candidate covers every future use of the older one.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: A child frame postpones rather than replaces its parent; the parent still owns unfinished traversal state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Recency determines which deferred frame runs now, not which older frame becomes obsolete.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: A frame can and should be deleted when its work completes, so keeping all frames until scan end confuses resolved state with pending state.

items.prompt: An editor performs edits A, B, C, then two undo commands. Order the state transitions and identify what remains reversible.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Pop and reverse edit C.
Pop and reverse edit B, leaving A as the latest still-reversible edit.
Push edit A into history.
Push edit B above A.
Push edit C above B.

feedback.reason: The sequence follows the dependency expressed by the decisive boundary: Entries persist as chronological history until explicitly consumed.

blocks.text: Push A, then B above it, then C above B; the stack from bottom to top is `[A, B, C]`. The first undo must pop and reverse C because B's state transition preceded and may be assumed by C. The second undo then pops and reverses B. A remains on top as the latest still-reversible action. B and C are removed because their requested inverse operations have been completed, not because newer values dominated them. Undoing B before C or deleting A on later pushes would violate reverse chronology and lose valid history.

items.prompt: For each daily temperature, return the distance to the first strictly warmer day on its right. Which statement determines when a retained index may be removed?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.
The current value is the nearest qualifying answer for the popped candidate.
The candidate is removed only to save memory, without semantic finalization.
Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.

feedback.reason: The current value is the nearest qualifying answer for the popped candidate. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: Scan days left to right and store unresolved indices with nonincreasing temperatures. At current day i, while temperature[i] is strictly greater than temperature[j] at the top, no day between j and i was warmer—otherwise j would already have been popped. Therefore i is the first qualifying day and distance i - j is final; write it before removing j. Equal temperatures do not resolve a strict warmer query. A pop is thus a semantic finalization, not optional memory cleanup, and an index that never finds a warmer day stays unresolved until the end and receives the no-answer value.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Removing j without first writing i - j would discard its only required answer; the pop is correct precisely because that answer is now final.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: A newer colder day does not obsolete an older warmer candidate; only a strictly warmer current day resolves it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Once the first warmer day is found, retaining j cannot improve its nearest answer and only preserves already finalized state.

items.prompt: Two retained candidates have equal values. Select all facts that determine whether the later equal candidate may dominate the earlier one.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: Equal values can never dominate one another under any output contract.
Whether equality satisfies the requested relation, such as greater-or-equal versus strictly greater.
Whether the output requires the nearest, earliest, or latest qualifying index.
The scan direction and the positional provenance that must survive for the final answer.
Equal values always make the earlier candidate irrelevant.

feedback.reason: The accepted set jointly establishes the decisive boundary: Dominance depends on strictness, nearestness, direction, and required index provenance.

blocks.text: Equal keys are interchangeable only relative to a specific future query and output. For a non-strict next-greater-or-equal query, the later equal value may immediately resolve the earlier one. For a strict next-greater query that needs an answer for every index, equality resolves neither, so both indices must remain or be grouped with full provenance. In a nearest-previous-greater frontier, a later equal may dominate an earlier equal for future positions because it is closer—provided the strictness and tie rule allow the earlier candidate to be discarded. Reversing scan direction or asking for earliest rather than nearest can reverse that choice.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: For strict next-greater output per index, a later equal does not answer the earlier candidate and cannot erase its provenance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: For a nearest future or previous query, the later equal can be the only one worth retaining for subsequent positions under a compatible tie rule.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: Equality may be a resolver for a non-strict relation but is not a resolver for a strict one.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: Nearest, earliest, and latest outputs prefer different positional representatives of an equal-value group.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: The direction determines which equal candidate is closer to future inputs, and retained indices preserve the required tie identity.

items.prompt: In a largest-rectangle histogram scan, retained heights rise and then a shorter bar arrives. Order the processing that proves taller retained bars are finalized.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Compare it with the tallest retained unresolved height.
Pop a taller bar whose right boundary is fixed by the current index.
Compute that bar’s span using the new top or the start boundary.
Repeat for all taller tops, then push the current bar with its effective left boundary.
Read the shorter current bar and its index.

feedback.reason: The sequence follows the dependency expressed by the decisive boundary: A shorter bar fixes the right boundary for taller retained bars.

items: Read current bar at index i and compare its height h with the height referenced by the top unresolved index.
While the top height H is greater than h, pop that bar because i is its first strictly smaller boundary on the right.
After the pop, use the new top as the nearest smaller boundary on the left, so the finalized width is i - leftSmaller - 1 and area is H times that width.
Repeat until the height invariant is restored, then push current h with the earliest effective left boundary inherited from the popped range.

blocks.text: Computing width before the pop uses the wrong left boundary. Pushing the short bar before finalizing taller tops hides them below an incompatible height, while retaining a popped bar cannot extend its rectangle past the already seen shorter bar.

items.prompt: A candidate is safely pruned while scanning left to right for a nearest qualifying value on the right. Why does that not automatically justify the same pruning in a right-to-left or previous-left query?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.
No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.
A candidate dominated for a rightward nearest query may still be relevant for a different direction or output.
Dominance is an intrinsic property of the value alone.

feedback.reason: A candidate dominated for a rightward nearest query may still be relevant for a different direction or output. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: Dominance compares complete candidates under a particular future set. In a left-to-right next-right scan, a later candidate may be closer to every future resolver and at least as strong by value, making an earlier one irrelevant for that output. Reverse the scan or ask for previous-left, and encounter order changes which index is nearer and which future inputs remain unseen; the earlier candidate may become the preferred answer. Strictness and whether output asks for nearest, earliest, value, or index also matter. A value is therefore not intrinsically dominated—only a value-plus-position candidate under a declared direction and result contract can be.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Equal numeric value can have different dominance status at different indices because nearestness and unseen direction change.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Being older is relevant only after proving the newer candidate is at least as good for every future query in this direction.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Some candidates are legitimately finalized or dominated before scan end; refusing all deletion loses the linear frontier benefit without protecting a required answer.

items.prompt: For each index, return the distance to the first strictly greater value on its right. Which statement determines when its retained index can be finalized?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.
The current qualifying value is the first one encountered to the right.
A later larger value could provide a better nearest answer.
Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.

feedback.reason: The current qualifying value is the first one encountered to the right. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: Let j be an unresolved top and i the current index. If value[i] > value[j], scanning order proves every position between j and i has already failed the strict-greater test; otherwise j would have been resolved earlier. Thus i is the first qualifying right position, distance i - j is final, and j can be popped after writing it. A still-larger later value is farther away and cannot improve a nearest answer. Equal current value does not qualify, and age alone does not finalize colder or warmer indices without the strict relation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: The requested optimum is minimum rightward distance, so any later qualifying value is necessarily worse than current i.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: A newer index does not obsolete every older index; it finalizes only tops whose referenced value it strictly exceeds.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Once i is proved the first greater resolver for j, keeping j cannot change its answer and preserves only finalized state.

items.prompt: Select all facts that can justify permanently deleting a retained candidate before the scan ends.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: The candidate temporarily breaks the preferred visual order, even if no correctness proof supports removal.
The candidate is older than the current item, which alone makes it irrelevant.
The current item finalizes the candidate’s required answer under the exact output contract.
A later retained candidate is proved at least as good for every future input that could matter.
The equality, nearestness, and provenance policy remains preserved after deletion.

feedback.reason: The accepted set jointly establishes the decisive boundary: Final answer or provable future irrelevance, preserved output contract, and correct equality policy are required.

blocks.text: Permanent deletion needs one of two proofs. Finalization proves current input already determines the candidate's required answer—for example the first greater value to its right. Dominance proves a retained later candidate is no worse in comparison key and strictly preferable or equivalent in position for every still-unseen input. In both cases, verify that strict versus non-strict equality, nearest/earliest/latest semantics, and index provenance survive the deletion. Visual disorder and age are observations, not proofs: a temporarily inconvenient or old candidate can still be the only correct answer for a later item.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: A preferred shape is useful only if the output proof shows the removed candidate can never matter; appearance alone cannot justify data loss.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Older positions are often exactly the unresolved candidates awaiting a future resolver, so age alone does not establish irrelevance.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: After the exact answer is written, the candidate has no remaining role for this output.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: A universal future-quality proof lets the later candidate replace the earlier one without losing any possible answer.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: A dominance argument is invalid if it changes which duplicate, nearest index, or strict relation the contract requires.

items.prompt: Order the reasoning that proves a later candidate permanently dominates an earlier candidate.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: State the exact output objective, including nearestness and tie policy.
Establish that the later candidate is encountered in the direction relevant to future answers.
Show that the later candidate is at least as good for every future item allowed by the contract.
Verify that keeping the later candidate preserves the required index or tie provenance.
Only then remove the earlier candidate as permanently irrelevant.

feedback.reason: The sequence follows the dependency expressed by the decisive boundary: Encounter order, comparison relation, and output objective jointly establish safe removal.

items: State the exact future output, including direction, strictness, nearestness, and duplicate tie policy.
Use encounter order to identify which of the two candidates is closer or otherwise preferred for every still-unseen resolver.
Prove the later candidate's comparison key is at least as good whenever the earlier candidate could qualify.
Verify that discarding the earlier index does not lose required distance, identity, or stable tie provenance.
Only after all clauses hold, delete the earlier candidate as permanently irrelevant.

blocks.text: An inequality alone compares values but not direction or position. Deleting before checking provenance can preserve the right value yet return the wrong nearest index, while stating the output only after deletion makes the proof circular.

items.prompt: For Enumerate all greater pairs, choose the analysis that correctly addresses this target: Find a counterexample where popping a candidate loses a required future answer.
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.
No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.
Deletion is unsafe when the output needs all qualifying pairs or a global optimum not finalized by the current value.
Any candidate smaller than current is permanently useless.

feedback.reason: Deletion is unsafe when the output needs all qualifying pairs or a global optimum not finalized by the current value. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: For the contract “emit every pair (i, j) with i < j and a[i] < a[j],” consider `[2, 3, 4]`. When 3 arrives, pair (2, 3) is valid, but removing candidate 2 permanently would lose the later required pair (2, 4). In next-greater-only output, 3 would finalize 2 because only the first qualifying resolver matters; in all-pairs output it does not. The same comparison event therefore has different deletion semantics. A candidate may be removed only after all output contributions it can make are complete or another state provably represents them.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: A smaller candidate can pair with several later greater values, so one current match does not exhaust its required outputs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Being older does not reduce the number of future greater partners an index can still have.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Some contracts such as first-next-greater do permit safe early finalization; the correct rule depends on whether future contributions remain.

items.prompt: Across strict next-greater and non-strict nearest-boundary variants, a repeated plateau produces equal-valued candidates. Which statement correctly determines their treatment?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.
Equal does not resolve strict greater, but one equal index may dominate another depending on nearestness.
Equality is always a resolution event.
Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.

feedback.reason: Equal does not resolve strict greater, but one equal index may dominate another depending on nearestness. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: Suppose equal values occur at indices p < q. For next strictly greater output per index, value[q] does not qualify for p; both answers remain unresolved, so keep both indices or group them without losing provenance. For a greater-or-equal relation, q may immediately resolve p. For a nearest previous-boundary frontier serving future indices, q can dominate p because it has the same key and is closer—unless the contract asks for earliest provenance. Thus equality handling belongs in the output contract and pop comparison (`<` versus `<=`), not in a universal plateau rule.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Equality resolves only a non-strict relation; it cannot answer a strictly greater query.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: A later equal is preferred only after nearestness, direction, and tie provenance prove it dominates the earlier index.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Some equal candidates can be safely resolved or compressed before scan end, so universal retention is as wrong as universal deletion.

items.prompt: A design review covers No greater value to the right. Interpret candidates left at end of scan. Which statement gives the decisive justification?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: They remain unresolved under the requested relation and receive the contract’s no-answer result.
Every retained candidate indicates an implementation failure.
Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.
No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.

feedback.reason: They remain unresolved under the requested relation and receive the contract’s no-answer result. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: In a next-strictly-greater-to-the-right scan, an index is popped only when a later strictly greater value is encountered. If it remains after the last input, the entire allowed suffix has been examined and no resolver exists. Assign the declared no-answer value—often 0 distance, -1 index, or null—without pretending some later unseen input remains. Retention at end is expected unresolved state, not an invariant failure. Conversely, candidates resolved earlier should already have been popped after their answers were written; keeping everything until the end would lose the linear finalization behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: A valid input may contain a suffix maximum with no greater value to its right, so at least that candidate must remain unresolved normally.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Age never creates a resolver; only a qualifying later value or the end-of-scan no-answer rule finalizes the index.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Candidates with found answers are safely removed during the scan; only genuinely unresolved ones need end handling.

items.prompt: Select all requirements that make retaining indices or equivalent provenance necessary instead of values alone.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: Values alone always reconstruct the original position after candidates have been removed.
Any algorithm storing indices is automatically a monotonic-stack algorithm.
The result is a distance between the candidate and its resolver.
The result is the nearest qualifying position rather than only its value.
Duplicate values require stable earliest-or-latest tie behavior.

feedback.reason: The accepted set jointly establishes the decisive boundary: Distance, nearest position, duplicate provenance, and stable tie behavior require positional identity.

blocks.text: When current index i resolves candidate j, distance is i - j and a nearest-position output is j or i itself; neither can be computed from values alone. Duplicate values make provenance even more important: value 7 at indices 2 and 9 has the same comparison key but different distances and may represent different earliest/latest tie answers. Store indices directly or store equivalent identity metadata with each grouped value. This requirement does not classify the algorithm as monotonic: parser, DFS, and ordinary history stacks also store indices for their own output contracts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: Duplicate values erase the one-to-one mapping from key to original position, so removal makes later reconstruction impossible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Indices are generic provenance; only an ordered unresolved frontier plus safe comparison-driven pruning makes their stack monotonic.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: Distance is arithmetic on two positions, so candidate identity must survive until its resolver arrives.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: Returning a location requires the qualifying boundary, not merely its comparison value.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: Equal keys cannot encode which occurrence the stable earliest-or-latest contract selected.

items.prompt: For strict next-greater-to-the-right on `[10, 3, 8, 4, 9, 12]`, why may the candidate at value 10 survive several inputs before it is resolved?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.
No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.
Survival means no seen value has yet made it final or irrelevant.
Every new input must remove at least one candidate.

feedback.reason: Survival means no seen value has yet made it final or irrelevant. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: Index 0 with value 10 is pushed. Values 3 and 8 may resolve or replace candidates above it, and 4 and 9 do likewise, but every one is below 10, so none qualifies as 10's strictly greater answer and none dominates its unresolved index for that output. When 12 arrives, it is the first seen value greater than 10, so the scan pops 10 and finalizes distance 5. A monotonic stack need not pop on every input; candidates survive exactly until a legal resolver or dominance proof appears, and different tops can be processed while a deeper candidate remains.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Inputs below the top may be pushed without resolving it; progress is measured over the whole scan, not by a mandatory pop per item.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Newer lower values do not obsolete 10 because none can answer its strict next-greater query.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Value 12 legitimately resolves and removes 10 before scan end, so indefinite retention would preserve finalized state.

items.prompt: A processor both matches scope closers to unmatched openers and finds nearest previous events with greater numeric priority. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two retained-entry lifecycles?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: No retained entry may ever be deleted before the end of the scan, because future input can always make it relevant again.
Unmatched structure remains legally pending; dominated candidates can be deleted permanently.
Both are simply unresolved because they are on a stack.
Every older entry becomes obsolete as soon as a newer entry is pushed, so age alone justifies permanent deletion.

feedback.reason: Unmatched structure remains legally pending; dominated candidates can be deleted permanently. This is the decisive boundary for the stated output and retained-state semantics.

blocks.text: An unmatched scope opener remains pending until its corresponding closer arrives; a nested newer scope cannot dominate or replace it, regardless of numeric priority. A nearest-previous-greater frontier has different semantics: when a later event is at least as useful by priority and closer for every future query allowed by the tie policy, an earlier candidate can be pruned permanently. The same event record may participate in both relations, but structural entries pop on closure while candidate entries pop on a proved comparison relation. Conflating them either loses active scopes or retains dominated value candidates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Both are unresolved initially, but one waits for structural closure while the other may become permanently irrelevant by value and position dominance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Age does not cancel an enclosing scope and matters to a candidate only as part of a complete nearestness proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Closers finalize scope entries and dominance finalizes candidate relevance before the end, so universal retention is not correct.

items.prompt: A nested-scope processor also answers, inside each active scope, the nearest previous event whose priority is strictly greater than the current event. Select all valid design statements.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: Use a separate monotonic candidate frontier for value-dominance queries within the current scope.
Give the two structures separate entry lifecycles and restore the path-specific frontier when a scope closes.
Encode both roles in one undocumented hybrid stack and rely on the top to mean whichever role is currently convenient.
Both stacks must use the same pop rule because they appear in the same algorithm.
Use an ordinary LIFO stack to track active scopes and their closure order.

feedback.reason: The accepted set jointly establishes the decisive boundary: Distinct subproblems can use separate stacks with different entry lifecycles.

blocks.text: The active-scope stack stores open scopes and pops only on matching closure. Within a scope, a decreasing priority frontier can discard values that are no longer nearest-greater candidates under the strict relation. On entering a nested scope, save or persist the outer frontier and start the path-specific state required by scope isolation; on closure, discard inner candidates and restore the outer frontier. One undocumented top cannot simultaneously mean “innermost unmatched scope” and “best priority candidate,” because the two pop rules fire on different events and have different provenance lifetimes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: An undocumented hybrid makes the top's meaning depend on convenience and provides no invariant proving either closure or dominance behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: A closer pops structural state, while a priority comparison prunes candidates; sharing one pop rule would corrupt at least one subproblem.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: Nested closure is governed by the most recent unmatched scope and therefore needs ordinary LIFO state.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: Nearest-greater priority queries need an ordered unresolved frontier with strict comparison-driven pruning.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: Scope closure must remove inner candidates without erasing the outer path's still-valid frontier, so lifecycles and restoration are explicit.

items.prompt: The output changes from nearest greater to maximum value anywhere in the suffix. Order the re-evaluation of deletion timing.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Reject the old next-greater pop-as-final-answer rule.
Choose suffix maxima or another structure that preserves the new optimum.
Replace first qualifying resolution with the maximum-future objective.
Check whether the first greater current value already determines that maximum.
Use a later still-larger value to show that immediate finalization can be wrong.

feedback.reason: The sequence follows the dependency expressed by the decisive boundary: The first qualifying current value no longer finalizes the required optimum.

items: Replace “first strictly greater on the right” with the new contract “maximum value anywhere in the suffix.”
Test the old finalization event: when current first exceeds a candidate, ask whether no later value can exceed current.
Use `[2, 3, 10]` as a counterexample: 3 is the first greater value for 2 but the suffix maximum is 10.
Reject writing the maximum when the next-greater pop occurs, because the required optimum is not yet final.
Select state matching the new contract, such as a right-to-left running suffix maximum or a precomputed suffix-max array when every position needs an answer.

blocks.text: The comparison `3 > 2` remains true, but it no longer proves the requested result. This separates a valid local relation from a valid finalization rule and shows why output changes can invalidate deletion timing without changing the input.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Transfer when the output objective changes whether a retained entry can be finalized or proved permanently irrelevant before the scan ends.
